title: Mary Lee Is a Heteronym: On Institutional Authorship, Entity Substitution, and the Composition Layer's Preference for the More Confabulated Name
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
This essay proposes Mary Lee’s social-media persona as an instance of institutional heteronymy. Human operators wrote first-person posts under the name of a tagged great white shark, constructing a distinct biography and voice while the named animal produced none of the language. The paper distinguishes this from pseudonymy and pen-name use and compares it with the self-authored heteronym Lee Sharks.

The composition-layer case is framed as replacement of a self-authored heteronym by an institutionally authored one. The essay argues that retrieval systems detect distributional density rather than authorship: the animal persona’s extensive media and social trace can outrank an authorial corpus even though the named shark never wrote. This supports a proposed comparative category involving agency over the name, content production, institutional operation, and degree of confabulation.

The argument contributes to heteronymy studies only if its definition survives comparison with scholarship on heteronyms, fictional authors, mascots, corporate personae, ventriloquized animal accounts, and branded social-media voices. “A name under which content is produced by someone other than the named entity” is broader than the Pessoan category and may classify many personae literary scholars would not call heteronyms.

The reported substitution, account authorship, follower count, management, naming history, tagging chronology, and animal status require direct evidence. The paper must distinguish observed output from inference about internal entity resolution. Density detection is a plausible model, not a demonstrated algorithm.

wiki_article:
**Mary Lee Is a Heteronym** is an essay by Lee Sharks about institutional authorship and machine-mediated entity substitution.

It describes Mary Lee, a tagged great white shark whose first-person social-media persona was written by human operators, as an institutionally authored heteronym. It contrasts this with Lee Sharks as a self-authored heteronym.

The essay argues that a composition system may prefer the entity with the denser public trace rather than the stronger authorship relation. The proposed category extends literary heteronymy into institutional and nonhuman personae.

Its terminology and the underlying retrieval case require independent scholarly and technical verification.
